beats.text: It was not a rogue algorithm.
beats.note: The SEC order traces it to a deployment slip. A technician did not copy the new code to one of eight servers, and no second person reviewed the job.
The new code reused a flag that once switched on Power Peg. Knight had stopped using Power Peg in 2003, but the code was still there and still callable.
Seven servers ran the new code correctly. The eighth still ran the old, and it began sending child orders from 212 parent orders.
The system sent 97 automated messages, starting around 8:01 a.m., saying Power Peg disabled. The order says staff generally did not review them.
Across 154 stocks and more than 397 million shares. Knight ended up about 3.5 billion dollars net long in 80 stocks and 3.15 billion short in 74.

beats.context: What Knight lost on those unwanted positions, according to the SEC order. One server out of eight.

beats.text: Seven servers were right. The eighth was enough.
